title: Neurocritical Care & Neurosurgical Pharmacology
summary: Drugs used around the injured brain and in the neurosurgical patient.

lessons.title: Intracranial Pressure and Osmotherapy

levels.kid:
When someone bumps their head really hard, the brain can swell, like a sponge soaking up water.

But the brain lives inside a hard box: the skull. The box cannot stretch. So when the brain swells, the squeeze inside gets bigger. Doctors call that squeeze **pressure**.

Too much squeeze is dangerous because blood has a harder time getting in to feed the brain.

One trick doctors use is a very salty or sugary liquid that goes into the blood. Water likes to move toward the salty side, so it slowly leaves the swollen brain and goes into the blood. The brain shrinks a little, and the squeeze goes down.

It is like putting salt on a cucumber slice to pull the water out.
levels.hs:
The skull is a rigid box holding three things: brain tissue, blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). This idea is the **Monro–Kellie doctrine**: if one gets bigger (a swollen brain, a blood clot), something else must shrink, or the pressure inside, the **intracranial pressure (ICP)**, rises.

Why it matters: blood flow to the brain depends on **cerebral perfusion pressure**:
- **CPP = MAP − ICP** (mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure).
If ICP climbs, CPP falls and brain cells starve of oxygen. Very high ICP can push brain tissue through openings in the skull, called **herniation**, which can be fatal.

**Osmotherapy** uses solutions that raise the concentration of particles in the blood. Because the intact blood–brain barrier blocks those particles, water moves out of the brain by osmosis and ICP falls. The two main agents are:
- **Mannitol**, a sugar alcohol that also makes the kidneys pass more urine.
- **Hypertonic saline**, concentrated salt water.

Other ICP tools include raising the head of the bed, sedation, draining CSF through a tube called an external ventricular drain, briefly breathing faster to shrink blood vessels, and in severe cases surgery to remove part of the skull.

Steroids reduce swelling around brain tumors, but they do not help after head injury.
levels.college:
**Physiology.** Normal adult ICP is roughly 5–15 mmHg. Brain Trauma Foundation guidance treats sustained ICP above about 22 mmHg after severe TBI and targets CPP around 60–70 mmHg. Autoregulation normally keeps cerebral blood flow stable across a range of CPP, but it is often impaired after injury, making flow pressure-passive.

**How osmotherapy works.** Effective osmotherapy requires an osmole the BBB excludes. The **reflection coefficient** (σ) describes this: sodium has σ close to 1, mannitol slightly lower (about 0.9), urea much lower. Raising serum osmolality creates a gradient that draws water from brain interstitium, mainly from regions with an intact barrier, which is why normal brain shrinks more than injured brain.

**Mannitol.**
- Acts within minutes partly through **rheology**: it expands plasma, lowers blood viscosity and hematocrit, and reflex vasoconstriction (with intact autoregulation) reduces cerebral blood volume.
- Then the slower osmotic effect follows.
- It is an **osmotic diuretic**: it causes volume depletion and hypotension (which lowers CPP), electrolyte loss and acute kidney injury when it accumulates.
- Accumulation is monitored with the **osmolar gap** (measured minus calculated osmolality).

**Hypertonic saline (HTS).**
- Raises serum sodium and osmolality without diuresis, so it supports blood pressure; useful in hypotensive or hypovolemic patients.
- Risks: hypernatremia, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, volume overload, and **osmotic demyelination** if a patient with chronic hyponatremia is corrected too fast. Concentrated forms need central venous access.

**Corticosteroids.** Dexamethasone reduces **vasogenic edema** around tumors and abscesses by tightening leaky tumor vessels. In TBI, the CRASH trial showed methylprednisolone *increased* mortality, so steroids are contraindicated there.

**Tiered therapy.** Head elevation, sedation and analgesia, CSF drainage, osmotherapy, then brief hyperventilation, barbiturate coma or decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP.
levels.phd:
**Edema types and drug targets.** Cytotoxic edema (cell swelling from energy failure, e.g., ischemia) occurs with an intact barrier; vasogenic edema reflects BBB breakdown with protein-rich fluid in the extracellular space; ionic edema, the transitional stage, involves sodium movement across a still-intact endothelium. Osmotherapy acts across intact BBB, so it mainly dehydrates normal brain, buying intracranial compliance rather than reversing the lesion. Steroids target vasogenic edema; they do little to cytotoxic edema.

**SUR1–TRPM4 channel.** After ischemia or trauma, endothelial and neural cells upregulate a SUR1-regulated nonselective cation channel. Its opening drives ionic and cytotoxic edema and can progress to hemorrhagic conversion. **Glibenclamide (glyburide)**, a sulfonylurea, blocks SUR1. An IV formulation reduced midline shift in phase II large hemispheric infarction trials, but the phase III CHARM trial did not show a clear functional benefit overall; TBI contusion studies continue.

**Mannitol rebound.** With repeated use, mannitol can leak into injured brain where the barrier is disrupted, reversing the gradient. The magnitude of this effect in humans is debated.

**Mannitol versus HTS.** Meta-analyses suggest HTS lowers ICP somewhat more effectively and for longer per equiosmolar load, but no trial has convincingly shown better long-term functional outcome. Choice often follows physiology: HTS for hypotension or hyponatremia, mannitol when hypernatremia limits HTS.

**Hyperventilation.** Hypocapnia raises perivascular pH, causing arteriolar vasoconstriction and reduced cerebral blood volume. The ICP drop is quick, but the CO2 response adapts over hours as CSF bicarbonate compensates, and aggressive hypocapnia can cause ischemia, so it is reserved as a short bridge.

**Barbiturates.** Pentobarbital lowers the cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen (CMRO2) and, through flow–metabolism coupling, blood volume and ICP. It is titrated to EEG burst suppression; hypotension and immunosuppression limit it. Trials (e.g., DECRA, RESCUEicp) show craniectomy lowers ICP and mortality but leaves more survivors severely disabled, framing an outcome trade-off rather than a cure.
levels.expert:
**How a neurointensivist thinks about a high ICP.**

First, exclude a surgical lesion. A rising ICP with a new hematoma or hydrocephalus needs a CT and a neurosurgeon, not more osmolality. Check the basics: head midline and elevated, nothing compressing the neck veins, adequate sedation, no fever, no seizures on EEG, normal CO2, and an EVD that is open and properly levelled.

**Choosing the osmotic agent.**
- **Hypotensive or hypovolemic patient:** hypertonic saline, because mannitol's diuresis can drop MAP and CPP.
- **Already hypernatremic:** mannitol, or accept the limit. Many units cap serum sodium somewhere in the 155–160 mmol/L range.
- **Acute kidney injury:** caution with mannitol; follow the osmolar gap. A gap over roughly 20 mOsm/kg suggests mannitol is accumulating and the next bolus should wait.
- Bolus therapy treats crises. Prophylactic continuous HTS targeting a sodium range did not improve outcome in the COBI trial.

**Pitfalls.**
- Sodium "overshoot" then rapid fall can worsen edema. Avoid letting sodium drop quickly once raised, and avoid hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose in water in brain injury.
- Chronic hyponatremia (e.g., an older patient with SIADH) plus HTS risks osmotic demyelination; correction should be deliberate.
- Measured osmolality, not only calculated, matters with mannitol.
- Hyperchloremia from HTS can cause non-anion-gap acidosis; sodium acetate mixtures are sometimes used.

**Steroids, revisited.**
- Metastasis with edema: dexamethasone works within hours. Taper once the cause is treated, and remember it can shrink CNS lymphoma, so biopsy before steroids when lymphoma is suspected.
- TBI: no steroids (CRASH).
- Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: no benefit.

**When to escalate.** If ICP stays high despite tier-one and tier-two measures, the next step is a team decision: barbiturate coma (with EEG and invasive blood pressure support) or decompressive craniectomy, framed honestly with family around the DECRA and RESCUEicp trade-off: more survival, but not always good-quality survival.

keyPoints: Monro–Kellie: brain, blood and CSF share a rigid skull; CPP = MAP − ICP
Osmotherapy works because the intact BBB excludes the osmole (high reflection coefficient)
Mannitol: rheologic then osmotic effect; osmotic diuresis, hypotension, AKI; follow the osmolar gap
Hypertonic saline: no diuresis, supports MAP; risks hypernatremia, hyperchloremic acidosis, osmotic demyelination
Dexamethasone helps vasogenic tumor edema; steroids increase mortality in TBI (CRASH)
Refractory ICP: brief hyperventilation, barbiturate burst suppression, decompressive craniectomy

test.q: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals:
test.explain: CPP = MAP − ICP, so rising ICP lowers CPP even if blood pressure is unchanged.

test.q: Why does osmotherapy shrink the brain?
choices: Osmotic agents increase cerebrospinal fluid production
Osmotic agents directly kill edematous brain cells
Osmotic agents block neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels
The intact BBB keeps the osmole in the blood, so water leaves brain tissue
test.explain: Water follows the osmotic gradient across an intact barrier that the solute cannot cross.

test.q: Which effect of mannitol makes it risky in a hypotensive patient?
choices: Reflex bradycardia after acute volume expansion
Seizures due to altered cortical ion channels
test.explain: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic; fluid loss can drop MAP and therefore CPP.

test.q: Which agent raises osmolality without causing a diuresis?
test.explain: Hypertonic saline expands intravascular volume rather than causing diuresis.

test.q: In severe traumatic brain injury, corticosteroids:
choices: Increased mortality in the CRASH trial
Rapidly reverse herniation from cytotoxic edema
test.explain: CRASH showed higher mortality with methylprednisolone, so steroids are not used in TBI.

test.q: Dexamethasone is useful for which kind of edema?
choices: Vasogenic edema around a brain tumor
test.explain: Steroids tighten leaky tumor vessels and reduce vasogenic edema.

test.q: A rising osmolar gap in a patient on repeated mannitol suggests:
test.explain: Unmeasured mannitol widens the gap between measured and calculated osmolality, signalling accumulation and kidney risk.

test.q: Why is hyperventilation only a short bridge?
choices: It causes lasting pain from overworked breathing muscles rather than cerebral vascular effects
It consistently raises ICP through cerebral vasodilation
Its effect fades as CSF bicarbonate compensates, and too much causes ischemia
It increases serum sodium beyond the safe range
test.explain: Hypocapnic vasoconstriction lowers blood volume but adapts over hours and can starve tissue of flow.

test.q: Name the doctrine stating that brain, blood and CSF share a fixed skull volume.
test.explain: The Monro–Kellie doctrine explains why any added volume raises ICP once compensation is used up.

test.q: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol that acts as an osmotic ___.
test.explain: It is filtered and not reabsorbed, so it pulls water into the urine.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for pressure inside the skull?
test.explain: Intracranial pressure.

test.q: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too quickly with hypertonic saline risks osmotic ___.
test.explain: Osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) follows overly rapid sodium correction in chronic hyponatremia.

kidTest.q: The skull is like a:
kidTest.explain: The skull cannot stretch, so swelling raises the squeeze inside.

kidTest.q: When the brain swells, the pressure inside the head:
kidTest.explain: More stuff in the same box means more squeeze.

kidTest.q: Why is too much pressure bad?
choices: Blood has a harder time feeding the brain
It makes your body grow much taller
It makes your hair grow very fast
kidTest.explain: High pressure makes it harder for blood to get in.

kidTest.q: A salty liquid in the blood pulls water:
kidTest.explain: Water moves toward the salty side, leaving the brain.

kidTest.q: Doctors call the squeeze inside the head ___.
kidTest.explain: Intracranial pressure is the squeeze inside the skull.

advancedTest.q: Why does osmotherapy shrink normal brain more than a contused region?
choices: The gradient acts across intact BBB; injured areas with disrupted barrier let the osmole in
Contused brain starts out dehydrated relative to intact tissue and therefore has less water available to remove
Normal brain has more sodium channels that attract osmoles
Contused tissue has markedly less blood flow, preventing osmole delivery
advancedTest.explain: Where the barrier is broken, the osmole leaks in and the gradient is lost, so water comes mainly from intact tissue.

advancedTest.q: Which drug blocks SUR1, the regulator of the SUR1–TRPM4 channel implicated in post-ischemic edema?
advancedTest.explain: Glibenclamide blocks SUR1; IV trials in large hemispheric infarction reduced midline shift but phase III functional benefit was not clearly shown.

advancedTest.q: A hypotensive TBI patient with ICP crises and normal sodium. The better first osmotic choice is:
choices: Dexamethasone because it reduces traumatic edema quickly
Mannitol because the lower price improves cerebral perfusion
Hypotonic fluid because it increases brain water excretion
Hypertonic saline, because it supports intravascular volume
advancedTest.explain: HTS avoids the diuresis that would further lower MAP and CPP.

advancedTest.q: DECRA and RESCUEicp together suggest decompressive craniectomy for refractory ICP:
choices: Does not reduce mortality in refractory intracranial hypertension
Lowers mortality but increases survival with severe disability
Increases pressure inside the skull after removing bone
Consistently produces better neurologic function than medical therapy
advancedTest.explain: The trade-off is more survivors, some of them with severe disability, which must be discussed openly.

lessons.title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Pharmacology

levels.kid:
Sometimes a weak spot in a brain blood vessel bulges like a tiny balloon. If it pops, blood spills into the space around the brain. Doctors call this a **subarachnoid hemorrhage**.

First, surgeons fix the balloon so it can't bleed again, using a tiny clip or soft coils.

But there is a second danger. A few days later, the blood vessels near the spilled blood can squeeze tight, like a hose being pinched. Then parts of the brain don't get enough blood.

Doctors give a medicine called **nimodipine** to help protect the brain during those days. They also keep the patient's body filled with enough fluid and watch them very closely.
levels.hs:
A **subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)** is bleeding into the space between the brain and its thin covering, most often from a burst **aneurysm**. Patients often describe "the worst headache of my life."

Treatment happens in steps:
- **Before the aneurysm is secured:** control blood pressure with fast, adjustable IV drugs (such as nicardipine or labetalol) to lower the chance of rebleeding, and treat pain.
- **Secure the aneurysm:** a neurosurgeon clips it, or an interventional neuroradiologist fills it with coils from inside the vessel.
- **Watch for delayed problems** over the next two weeks.

The big delayed problem is **delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI)**, often linked to **vasospasm**: arteries near the blood clot narrow, usually between days 3 and 14. This can cause new weakness or confusion, like a stroke.

The key drug is **nimodipine**, a calcium channel blocker. It is the only drug shown to improve outcome after aneurysmal SAH. Interestingly, it does not clearly stop the arteries from narrowing; it seems to protect the brain in other ways.

Other problems include hydrocephalus (needs a drain), seizures, low blood sodium and heart strain. Patients are kept with normal fluid volume, not dried out.
levels.college:
**Early phase.** Rebleeding risk is highest in the first hours to day. Before securing the aneurysm, systolic pressure is usually kept below a target (often about 160 mmHg) using titratable agents: **nicardipine** or **clevidipine** (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) or **labetalol** (combined α1/β blocker). Nitroprusside is avoided because it dilates cerebral vessels and can raise ICP. A short course of **tranexamic acid** to prevent rebleeding was tested in the ULTRA trial and did not improve functional outcome.

**Nimodipine.**
- A lipophilic dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blocker with relative cerebrovascular selectivity.
- Given enterally in the US (an IV form exists in some countries). Started early and continued for about three weeks.
- Improves outcome in meta-analyses but does not reliably prevent angiographic vasospasm, so its benefit is thought to involve neuroprotection, improved microcirculation or reduced spreading depolarizations.
- Main side effect: **hypotension**, which can lower cerebral perfusion. Splitting the total into smaller, more frequent portions is a common workaround.
- Metabolized by **CYP3A4**: strong inducers (e.g., some antiseizure drugs) lower exposure; inhibitors raise it.

**Delayed cerebral ischemia.**
- Monitored with neuro exams, transcranial Doppler velocities and CT perfusion or angiography.
- Treatment of symptomatic DCI: **induced hypertension** with vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) after the aneurysm is secured, plus endovascular therapy: intra-arterial vasodilators (verapamil, nicardipine, milrinone) or balloon angioplasty for proximal vessels.
- The old "triple-H" therapy (hypertension, hypervolemia, hemodilution) has been abandoned: hypervolemia causes pulmonary edema without benefit. **Euvolemia** is the goal.

**Sodium problems.** Hyponatremia is common, from **cerebral salt wasting** (natriuresis with volume loss) or **SIADH**. Fluid restriction is avoided because hypovolemia worsens DCI. Treatment uses isotonic or hypertonic saline and sometimes **fludrocortisone** to limit sodium loss.

**Negative trials.** Magnesium (MASH-2) and statins (STASH) did not improve outcome.
levels.phd:
**Rethinking DCI.** The classic model blamed large-artery vasospasm caused by oxyhemoglobin and its breakdown products. Clinical data broke that link: **clazosentan**, an endothelin-A receptor antagonist, reduced angiographic vasospasm dose-dependently in CONSCIOUS-1 to -3, yet did not improve functional outcome, and caused pulmonary complications, hypotension and anemia. (It has been approved in Japan; REACT, a later trial, also missed its primary endpoint.) Infarcts also occur in territories without visible spasm.

The current model of DCI is multifactorial:
- **Early brain injury** in the first 72 hours from the transient global ischemia of the ictus (ICP spike to near arterial pressure).
- **Microvascular dysfunction:** microthrombosis, pericyte constriction of capillaries and loss of autoregulation.
- **Cortical spreading depolarizations (SDs):** waves of near-complete neuronal depolarization. In SAH, SDs can trigger an *inverse* hemodynamic response (vasoconstriction instead of hyperemia), producing spreading ischemia. Clusters of SDs on electrocorticography predict delayed infarcts.
- **Neuroinflammation,** including heme–TLR4 signaling and complement activation.

Nimodipine's benefit fits this broader model: it may limit SD-induced ischemia and calcium-mediated injury rather than reversing large-vessel narrowing.

**Investigational directions.** Intrathecal or intraventricular nimodipine and nicardipine (prolonged-release formulations); clot-clearing with lumbar drainage or intraventricular thrombolysis (EARLYDRAIN showed better outcome with lumbar drainage); cilostazol (a PDE3 inhibitor used mainly in Japan); heparin infusion (ASTROH trial); milrinone protocols (combined PDE3 inhibition with vasodilation and inotropy).

**Cardiac and pulmonary injury.** A catecholamine surge produces neurogenic stunned myocardium (Takotsubo-like wall motion, troponin release) and neurogenic pulmonary edema. These complicate induced hypertension, which raises myocardial demand.

**Methodological lesson.** SAH research illustrates the danger of surrogate endpoints: a drug can fix a picture (angiographic narrowing) without changing patient-centered outcomes.
levels.expert:
**The SAH ICU checklist an attending runs every morning.**

**Days 0–1.**
- Secure the aneurysm early, ideally within 24 hours.
- Blood pressure: titratable infusion (nicardipine or clevidipine) rather than repeated boluses. Avoid big swings.
- Start nimodipine on arrival. Hold or reduce it if it drops MAP; never "fix" nimodipine hypotension by giving it IV in a system where only the enteral form is approved, a known source of serious errors.
- Hydrocephalus: early EVD if the patient is drowsy. Avoid over-draining before the aneurysm is secured.
- Seizure prophylaxis: if used, a short course of levetiracetam. Avoid phenytoin, which is associated with worse cognitive outcome after SAH.

**Days 3–14, the DCI window.**
- Neuro exam at short intervals. In poor-grade patients who can't be examined, lean on CT perfusion, continuous EEG (falling alpha/delta ratio) or invasive monitoring.
- Transcranial Doppler velocities and the Lindegaard ratio (MCA/ICA velocity) separate vasospasm from hyperemia.
- **New deficit?** Rule out rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizure, hyponatremia, fever and hypoxia first. Then induce hypertension in steps and reassess the exam. If no improvement, angiography for intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty.

**Fluids and sodium.**
- Euvolemia guided by exam, fluid balance and sometimes dynamic indices. No prophylactic hypervolemia.
- Falling sodium plus high urine output suggests cerebral salt wasting: replace salt and volume, consider fludrocortisone. **Do not fluid restrict.**

**Drug interactions that bite.**
- Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine) reduce nimodipine exposure through CYP3A4.
- Vasopressor-induced hypertension on a heart with stunned myocardium: watch troponin, echo and lactate.

**Talking to families.** Explain that the danger period continues for about two weeks even after a successful clip or coil, so a good day 2 does not mean the patient is safe.

keyPoints: Before securing the aneurysm: titratable BP control (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol)
Nimodipine is the only drug shown to improve outcome; main side effect hypotension; CYP3A4 substrate
DCI peaks days 3–14; treat with induced hypertension and endovascular vasodilators or angioplasty
Triple-H abandoned: aim for euvolemia; never fluid restrict hyponatremia after SAH
Clazosentan reduced angiographic vasospasm without improving outcome: a surrogate endpoint lesson
Magnesium, statins and tranexamic acid failed to improve outcome in trials

test.explain: About 85% of spontaneous SAH comes from aneurysm rupture.

test.q: Which drug improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH?
test.explain: Nimodipine is the only drug with consistent outcome benefit.

test.q: Nimodipine belongs to which class?
choices: Endothelin receptor antagonist of the ETA subtype

test.q: The main dose-limiting side effect of nimodipine is:
test.explain: Vasodilation lowers MAP, which can reduce cerebral perfusion.

test.q: Delayed cerebral ischemia is most likely around:
choices: Within the hours of aneurysm repair
test.explain: Vasospasm and DCI typically occur between days 3 and 14.

test.q: Why was triple-H therapy abandoned?
choices: The regimen provoked seizures by lowering serum glucose
It was abandoned because the treatment cost was too high
It consistently reduced systemic blood pressure below baseline
Hypervolemia caused complications such as pulmonary edema without benefit

test.q: After SAH, a patient with low sodium and high urine output should:
choices: Restrict fluids to correct the sodium by increasing serum concentration
Withhold intravenous fluids to reduce cerebral edema
Use a diuretic to lower urinary sodium losses
test.explain: Cerebral salt wasting causes volume loss; restriction worsens DCI risk.

test.q: Why is nitroprusside avoided for blood pressure control before securing the aneurysm?
choices: It causes treatment-emergent hyperglycemia through β2 activation
It dilates cerebral vessels and can raise ICP
Its slow onset prevents rapid blood-pressure titration
Its fixed infusion rate prevents blood-pressure titration

test.explain: Raising perfusion pressure and dilating spastic vessels are the main tools.

test.explain: Vasospasm is associated with, but not identical to, delayed cerebral ischemia.

Inverse coupling with vasoconstriction and spreading ischemia
Cortical hyperemia without regional perfusion loss

advancedTest.explain: Enzyme inducers markedly reduce nimodipine exposure.

lessons.title: Seizure Prophylaxis After Brain Injury

levels.kid:
After a bad head injury or brain surgery, the brain's electricity can sometimes go haywire. That is called a **seizure**. It's like a storm of signals all firing at once.

Doctors know that seizures are most likely in the first week after an injury. So sometimes they give a medicine to calm the brain's electricity during that week, like putting a lid on a pot so it doesn't boil over.

A common one is **levetiracetam**. Another older one is **phenytoin**.

If a seizure keeps going and won't stop, that is an emergency. Doctors first give a fast calming medicine, then a stronger one if needed.
levels.hs:
**Seizures after brain injury** are split into two kinds:
- **Early seizures** happen in the first 7 days. They are caused by the acute injury itself (blood irritating the cortex, swelling, low oxygen).
- **Late seizures** happen after the first week and reflect scarring that can make the brain permanently prone to seizures, called **post-traumatic epilepsy**.

Early seizures are dangerous in an injured brain because they raise metabolic demand, blood flow and ICP. That's why many severe head-injury patients get a short course of **seizure prophylaxis** (preventive medicine) for 7 days.

A landmark 1990 trial showed that **phenytoin** cut early seizures after severe TBI, but it did **not** prevent late epilepsy. So longer prevention isn't recommended.

Today many hospitals use **levetiracetam** instead because it has few drug interactions and doesn't need blood level checks.

For brain tumors, patients who have never had a seizure usually aren't given long-term preventive drugs.

**Status epilepticus** (a seizure lasting more than about 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery) is an emergency:
1. A benzodiazepine first (lorazepam IV or midazolam into a muscle).
2. Then a second-line drug: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.
3. If it continues, anesthetic infusions in the ICU.
levels.college:
**Evidence base.** Temkin's 1990 RCT in severe TBI: phenytoin reduced early post-traumatic seizures (roughly 14% to 4%) without reducing late seizures. Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines recommend prophylaxis for 7 days. Similar logic (early benefit, no antiepileptogenesis) has been shown for valproate and carbamazepine.

**Phenytoin pharmacology.**
- Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels by stabilizing the **fast-inactivated** state, limiting high-frequency repetitive firing.
- **Michaelis–Menten (saturable) kinetics:** near therapeutic levels, small dose changes cause disproportionate level rises.
- Highly albumin-bound: in hypoalbuminemia or uremia, total levels underestimate the active free fraction, so measure **free phenytoin**.
- Potent inducer of CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and others; lowers levels of dexamethasone, nimodipine, many chemotherapeutics and anticoagulants.
- IV adverse effects: hypotension and arrhythmia (partly from the propylene glycol vehicle) and **purple glove syndrome** with extravasation. **Fosphenytoin**, a water-soluble phosphate prodrug, avoids the vehicle and allows faster, safer infusion.
- Chronic effects include gingival hyperplasia, ataxia, nystagmus and SJS/TEN (higher risk with HLA-B*15:02).

**Levetiracetam.**
- Binds **synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A)**, modulating neurotransmitter release.
- Renally cleared, minimal protein binding, no CYP induction; adjust for kidney function.
- Main adverse effects: irritability, mood changes, somnolence.
- Comparative studies suggest similar early-seizure prevention to phenytoin with fewer adverse events; high-quality RCT evidence is limited.

**Status epilepticus.** RAMPART showed IM midazolam is at least as effective as IV lorazepam prehospital. ESETT showed fosphenytoin, levetiracetam and valproate stop benzodiazepine-refractory status at similar rates (about half). Refractory status needs continuous midazolam or propofol infusions, or pentobarbital, with EEG guidance.

**Brain tumors.** Guidelines (AAN; SNO/ASCO 2021) advise against routine prophylaxis in seizure-naive patients; perioperative use is optional and should be stopped soon after surgery.
levels.phd:
**Epileptogenesis versus ictogenesis.** Every available antiseizure drug suppresses seizures (anti-ictogenic) but none has been proven to prevent the development of epilepsy (antiepileptogenic) in humans. After injury, a latent period involves:
- BBB disruption with **albumin extravasation**, which activates astrocytic **TGF-β signaling**, downregulates Kir4.1 and glutamate transporters and impairs potassium buffering.
- Neuroinflammation (IL-1β, HMGB1–TLR4).
- Iron from blood breakdown generating reactive oxygen species (cortical hemosiderin is a strong risk factor).
- Mossy fiber sprouting, interneuron loss and network reorganization.

**Candidate antiepileptogenic strategies** have shown promise in animals: losartan (blocking TGF-β signaling via the AT1 receptor), mTOR inhibitors (rapamycin), anti-inflammatory agents and **biomarker-guided trials** using EEG or imaging features. Translation is hampered by the long latent period and the low per-patient risk of epilepsy, which demands large trials.

**Nonconvulsive seizures.** Continuous EEG reveals nonconvulsive seizures in a substantial minority of comatose ICU patients (estimates vary widely across cohorts). They are associated with microdialysis evidence of metabolic crisis (raised lactate/pyruvate ratio, glutamate release) and with hippocampal atrophy, but whether treating them improves outcome remains debated. The **ictal–interictal continuum** (periodic discharges) creates diagnostic uncertainty; the 2HELPS2B score helps estimate seizure risk.

**Sodium channel pharmacology contrast.**
- Phenytoin and carbamazepine stabilize **fast inactivation** and show use-dependence.
- **Lacosamide** enhances **slow inactivation**, a mechanistically distinct target; it can prolong the PR interval.

**SV2A biology.** SV2A is a vesicle membrane glycoprotein involved in priming and calcium-sensitivity of exocytosis. Levetiracetam and brivaracetam (higher affinity, faster brain entry) bind it; SV2A PET ligands such as [11C]UCB-J are now used as markers of synaptic density in neurodegeneration research.

**Timing in status epilepticus.** As status persists, synaptic GABA-A receptors are internalized while NMDA receptors traffic to the membrane, explaining time-dependent benzodiazepine resistance and the rationale for early, adequate first-line treatment.
levels.expert:
**Practical prophylaxis decisions.**

- **Severe TBI:** 7 days, then stop unless the patient has seized. Levetiracetam is the usual choice; renal function guides the regimen. Don't let a "seizure prophylaxis" order roll on for months at discharge, a very common error.
- **Brain tumor, never seized:** no long-term prophylaxis. If started perioperatively, stop within about a week after surgery when there are no seizures.
- **Brain tumor with seizures:** prefer non-enzyme-inducing drugs (levetiracetam, lacosamide). Enzyme inducers reduce exposure to dexamethasone and many chemotherapeutics and complicate trial eligibility.
- **SAH:** brief if at all; avoid phenytoin.
- **Intracerebral hemorrhage:** no routine prophylaxis; treat clinical or EEG seizures.

**Phenytoin, if you must.**
- Interpret total levels against albumin, or order free levels.
- Saturable kinetics: small adjustments, then wait before re-checking, since time to steady state lengthens as levels rise.
- Watch for interactions both ways: it induces many drugs, and its own levels change with valproate (displacement and inhibition) and with feeding through some nasogastric tubes.
- Use fosphenytoin IV with cardiac monitoring.

**Levetiracetam pitfalls.**
- Behavioral effects (agitation, depression) can be mistaken for the brain injury itself. Pyridoxine is sometimes tried; switching agents is more reliable.
- Accumulates in renal failure; is removed by hemodialysis.

**Status epilepticus in neuro ICU.**
- Benzodiazepine early and adequately; underdosing is the most common failure.
- Second-line within minutes, not hours.
- Refractory status: intubate, infuse midazolam or propofol titrated to seizure suppression or burst suppression on continuous EEG, and look for the cause (hematoma growth, hyponatremia, infection, missed or stopped antiseizure medicines).
- Super-refractory status: consider other agents and the ketogenic diet, and keep looking for autoimmune encephalitis.
- Neuromuscular blockade stops the visible movements, not the seizure. Continuous EEG is mandatory when paralyzed.

keyPoints: Early post-traumatic seizures (first 7 days) are prevented by prophylaxis; late epilepsy is not
Phenytoin: fast-inactivation Na channel blocker, saturable kinetics, highly protein bound, potent CYP inducer
Levetiracetam binds SV2A, renally cleared, few interactions; behavioral side effects
Status epilepticus: benzodiazepine, then fosphenytoin/levetiracetam/valproate (ESETT), then anesthetic infusions
No routine long-term prophylaxis for seizure-naive brain tumor patients
No antiseizure drug is proven antiepileptogenic in humans

lessons.title: Sedation and Analgesia in Neurocritical Care

levels.kid:
When someone has a serious brain injury, they may need a breathing machine in the hospital. That can be scary and uncomfortable.

So doctors give medicines that keep them **comfortable**, **calm** and **not in pain**. Some medicines make them sleepy, and some take away pain.

But brain doctors have a special problem. They need to check the brain often by asking the patient to squeeze a hand or open their eyes. If the patient is too sleepy, the doctor can't tell how the brain is doing.

So doctors pick medicines that wear off quickly, like a light switch they can turn on and off, so they can wake the patient up to check on them.
levels.hs:
Patients in a neuro ICU are often on ventilators with injured brains. Sedation and pain control there have two jobs:
- **Comfort and safety:** treat pain, prevent agitation and fighting the ventilator.
- **Brain protection:** coughing, pain and agitation raise blood pressure, ICP and the brain's oxygen demand. Deep sedation lowers that demand.

But there is a trade-off: sedation hides the **neurological exam**, the doctor's main tool for spotting a new bleed or swelling. So neurointensivists favor short-acting drugs they can pause.

Common drugs:
- **Propofol:** a fast-on, fast-off sedative given as an infusion. It lowers brain metabolism and ICP. It can drop blood pressure.
- **Dexmedetomidine:** a calming drug that leaves patients easy to wake and doesn't stop breathing. It can slow the heart rate.
- **Midazolam:** a benzodiazepine that can build up over days, causing longer sleepiness and confusion.
- **Fentanyl** and **remifentanil:** opioid pain relievers. Remifentanil wears off within minutes.
- **Pentobarbital:** a barbiturate used for deep "barbiturate coma" when ICP can't be controlled otherwise.

The modern approach is **analgesia first**: treat pain properly, and many patients need much less sedative.
levels.college:
**Goals and tools.** Sedation depth is scored with scales such as RASS; pain with CPOT or BPS in non-verbal patients. In the neuro ICU, deeper targets may be justified while ICP is unstable; otherwise light sedation and analgesia-first strategies reduce ventilator days and delirium.

**Propofol.**
- Positive allosteric modulator of **GABA-A** receptors.
- Rapid redistribution and high clearance give a short **context-sensitive half-time**, allowing neuro exams soon after pausing.
- Reduces CMRO2, cerebral blood flow and ICP; anticonvulsant at higher depths.
- Causes vasodilation and myocardial depression → hypotension, which can lower CPP; often paired with vasopressors.
- **Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS):** metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, hypertriglyceridemia, arrhythmias and heart failure, with prolonged high-rate infusions; risk rises with catecholamines and steroids. Monitor CK, lactate and triglycerides.
- Lipid emulsion vehicle adds calories and can cause pancreatitis.

**Dexmedetomidine.**
- Selective central **α2-adrenergic agonist** acting on the **locus coeruleus**; produces "cooperative sedation" resembling natural sleep.
- Minimal respiratory depression; patients can be woken for an exam.
- Bradycardia and hypotension; a biphasic BP response with fast loading.
- May reduce delirium compared with benzodiazepines.

**Midazolam.** GABA-A modulator; with prolonged infusion it accumulates in fat, and its active metabolite (α-hydroxymidazolam glucuronide) accumulates in renal failure. Associated with delirium. Still useful for refractory status epilepticus.

**Opioids.**
- **Fentanyl:** lipophilic; context-sensitive half-time lengthens markedly with long infusions.
- **Remifentanil:** hydrolyzed by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases; offset in minutes regardless of infusion duration and independent of liver or kidney function. Ideal for scheduled neuro checks; risk of opioid-induced hyperalgesia after abrupt stop.

**Barbiturates.** Pentobarbital for refractory ICP, titrated to burst suppression; causes hypotension, ileus, immunosuppression and a prolonged effect that confounds neurological assessment.
levels.phd:
**Context-sensitive half-time (CSHT).** CSHT is the time for plasma concentration to fall 50% after stopping an infusion maintained for a given duration. It depends on redistribution from peripheral compartments, not elimination half-life alone. For fentanyl and midazolam, peripheral compartments fill during long infusions and then return drug to plasma, so CSHT climbs steeply. Propofol's CSHT rises more modestly, and remifentanil's stays flat because esterase clearance vastly exceeds distribution. For neuro exams, the relevant quantity is often the decrement to a concentration compatible with arousal, which can differ from 50%.

**Cerebral physiology of sedatives.**
- Propofol and barbiturates preserve flow–metabolism coupling: CMRO2 falls and cerebral blood flow falls with it, lowering cerebral blood volume and ICP. CO2 reactivity is maintained.
- Volatile anesthetics are direct cerebral vasodilators, which is one reason they are used cautiously when ICP is high.
- Dexmedetomidine reduces CBF somewhat more than CMRO2 in some studies, raising theoretical concerns about flow–metabolism mismatch in the injured brain; clinical significance remains uncertain.

**PRIS mechanism.** Propofol impairs mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation (inhibiting carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 and the electron transport chain), producing an energy crisis in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Catecholamines and corticosteroids increase lipolysis and fatty-acid load, and children and those with mitochondrial disorders are at higher risk.

**Neuro wake-up tests.** Interrupting sedation allows a clinical exam, but in patients with intracranial hypertension it can trigger ICP surges, raise catecholamines and lower brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2). Many units therefore avoid daily interruption in unstable patients and use multimodal monitoring instead.

**Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH).** After severe TBI, some patients develop episodic tachycardia, hypertension, fever, sweating and posturing, attributed to disconnection of inhibitory centers causing an excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio imbalance in spinal circuits. Treatment combines opioids, nonselective β-blockers (propranolol), α2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine), gabapentin and sometimes bromocriptine; it is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out infection and seizures.
levels.expert:
**How I set up sedation for a fresh severe TBI with an ICP monitor.**

- **Analgesia first:** an opioid infusion (fentanyl, or remifentanil if frequent exams are a priority).
- **Sedative:** propofol titrated to ICP and synchrony with the ventilator. Watch MAP: if CPP falls, fix it with a vasopressor rather than letting the ICP benefit cost perfusion.
- **Exam plan:** decide explicitly when the team will lighten sedation for an exam, and whether ICP is stable enough to do so.

**Monitoring for trouble.**
- **PRIS screen:** trend lactate, CK, potassium, triglycerides and ECG with prolonged or high-rate propofol, especially if the patient is also on vasopressors or steroids. Unexplained acidosis or new arrhythmia means stop propofol.
- **Accumulation:** a patient still unresponsive two days after stopping midazolam may simply be sedated. Check renal function and consider a benzodiazepine-free exam period before making prognostic statements.
- **Barbiturate coma:** confirm burst suppression on EEG rather than escalating blindly, and know that barbiturates confound brain-death testing for a long time after stopping. Ancillary tests (e.g., cerebral blood flow studies) or waiting for clearance are needed.

**Choosing between agents.**
- **Agitated but needs exams (e.g., post-op, frontal contusion):** dexmedetomidine; watch heart rate.
- **Refractory status epilepticus:** midazolam or propofol, guided by EEG.
- **Refractory ICP:** pentobarbital, only after tier-one and tier-two measures.
- **Need for paralysis:** neuromuscular blockers only with adequate sedation and continuous EEG, since paralysis hides seizures and awareness.

**Pitfalls seen in practice.**
- Treating agitation with more sedation when the cause is pain, hypoxia, a full bladder or a new hematoma.
- Abrupt cessation after long opioid or benzodiazepine infusions causing iatrogenic withdrawal symptoms; taper deliberately.
- Labelling episodic fever and tachycardia as PSH before excluding infection.

keyPoints: Neuro ICU sedation balances brain protection against losing the neurological exam
Propofol: GABA-A, short CSHT, lowers CMRO2 and ICP; hypotension; PRIS with prolonged high-rate use
Dexmedetomidine: α2 agonist at locus coeruleus, arousable sedation, little respiratory depression, bradycardia
Remifentanil is esterase-metabolized with a flat context-sensitive half-time
Midazolam accumulates; pentobarbital for refractory ICP titrated to burst suppression
Paralysis hides seizures: continuous EEG is required

lessons.title: Perioperative Anticoagulant Reversal

levels.kid:
Some people take medicine to stop their blood from clotting too easily. These are called **blood thinners**. They help prevent strokes and clots in the legs.

But if that person needs brain surgery, or has bleeding in the brain, the blood thinner becomes a problem. Their blood won't stop bleeding!

So doctors use special **reversal** medicines, like an "undo button" for the blood thinner.

Different blood thinners need different undo buttons. Some undo medicines grab the blood thinner and hold onto it so it can't work. Others give the body extra clotting helpers.

Doctors have to act fast, because bleeding in the brain can grow quickly.
levels.hs:
**Anticoagulants** ("blood thinners") prevent clots in conditions like atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves and deep vein thrombosis. But in a patient with a brain bleed or who needs urgent brain surgery, they can make bleeding much worse. Reversing them fast is one of the most time-critical jobs in neurosurgery.

Each drug has its own reversal strategy:
- **Warfarin** blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so the liver makes fewer working clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Reversal: **prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)**, a concentrate of those factors that works within minutes, plus **IV vitamin K** so the liver can make its own again.
- **Dabigatran** directly blocks thrombin. Reversal: **idarucizumab**, an antibody fragment that grabs dabigatran.
- **Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban** block factor Xa. Reversal: **andexanet alfa**, a fake factor Xa that soaks up the drug, or PCC.
- **Heparin**: **protamine**, a positively charged protein that binds the negatively charged heparin.
- **Antiplatelet drugs** like aspirin and clopidogrel have no true antidote. Platelet transfusion is sometimes used before surgery, but in one trial it made outcomes worse for patients with brain bleeds who didn't need surgery.

For planned (elective) surgery, doctors simply stop the drug a few days before, depending on kidney function and bleeding risk.
levels.college:
**Warfarin.**
- Inhibits **vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)**, so factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S are made without γ-carboxylation and are nonfunctional.
- **4-factor PCC** (factors II, VII, IX, X plus proteins C and S) corrects the INR within minutes and with far less volume than plasma. INCH (warfarin-associated ICH) showed faster INR correction and less hematoma growth with PCC than with fresh frozen plasma.
- **IV vitamin K** is essential because PCC factors are consumed over hours; without it the INR rebounds.

**Dabigatran.** Direct thrombin inhibitor, mostly renally cleared. **Idarucizumab** is a humanized monoclonal antibody **Fab fragment** binding dabigatran with much higher affinity than thrombin (RE-VERSE AD). Dabigatran is also partly dialyzable.

**Factor Xa inhibitors.**
- **Andexanet alfa:** recombinant, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds the inhibitors. ANNEXA-I (ICH within hours of symptom onset) showed better hemostatic efficacy than usual care, mostly PCC, but more thrombotic events, including ischemic stroke.
- **4F-PCC** is widely used where andexanet is unavailable or for cost reasons; evidence is mainly observational.
- Anti-Xa activity assays calibrated to the specific drug estimate residual effect; standard INR is unreliable.

**Heparins.** Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin but only partially reverses LMWH (it neutralizes the long chains, not the smaller anti-Xa fragments). Adverse effects include hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions, especially in people previously exposed to protamine-containing insulin or with fish allergy.

**Antiplatelets.** PATCH: platelet transfusion in spontaneous ICH on antiplatelets (non-surgical) increased death or dependence. For patients undergoing neurosurgery, transfusion is still often used; **desmopressin** (releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII) is an option.

**Thrombolytics.** Symptomatic ICH after alteplase or tenecteplase: stop the infusion, give **cryoprecipitate** (fibrinogen) and consider **tranexamic acid**.
levels.phd:
**Why reversal is hard for factor Xa inhibitors.** Andexanet binds inhibitor molecules stoichiometrically, so its effect lasts only as long as it is present; after the infusion, unbound inhibitor redistributing from tissues restores anti-Xa activity. Andexanet also binds **tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI)**, which removes a natural anticoagulant brake and may explain part of the thrombotic signal. It interferes with heparin activity, complicating anticoagulation for later cardiac bypass or ECMO.

**PCC as a non-specific strategy.** PCC raises substrate (prothrombin and other factors) to overcome inhibition rather than removing the drug. Its effect on factor Xa inhibitors is concentration-dependent and incomplete in laboratory studies. Activated PCC (FEIBA) and recombinant factor VIIa are more prothrombotic and generally avoided for DOAC reversal.

**Universal reversal agents.** **Ciraparantag** is a small synthetic molecule that binds heparins and DOACs through noncovalent interactions; it is still investigational, partly because whole-blood clotting time is the main measure of its effect.

**Measuring residual drug.** For dabigatran, the dilute thrombin time and ecarin clotting time correlate with concentration; a normal standard thrombin time essentially excludes a meaningful level. For factor Xa inhibitors, drug-calibrated anti-Xa assays work, but turnaround time often exceeds the window for decisions, so clinicians rely on time since last ingestion and renal function.

**Hematoma expansion biology.** Expansion occurs mostly in the first few hours after ICH and is a major determinant of outcome. The CT angiography "spot sign" predicts expansion. This early window explains why the speed of reversal (door-to-needle) matters, and why trials of hemostatic agents (rFVIIa in FAST, tranexamic acid in TICH-2) reduced growth modestly without a clear functional benefit overall, perhaps because treatment arrived too late in many patients.

**Restarting anticoagulation.** After ICH, the decision balances recurrent bleeding against thromboembolism. Observational data suggest resumption is often net beneficial in atrial fibrillation; trials comparing resumption with left atrial appendage occlusion and with no anticoagulation are ongoing or recently reported.
levels.expert:
**The phone call: "Anticoagulated patient with an acute subdural, needs the OR."**

**Get the facts in parallel, not in series.**
- Which drug, and when was the last ingestion? Ask the family, check the pharmacy record, look at the pill bottle.
- Renal function (DOAC clearance), platelet count, INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, and drug-specific levels if available quickly.
- Indication for anticoagulation: a mechanical mitral valve or a recent clot changes how much you worry about reversing.

**Reverse by drug.**
- **Warfarin:** 4F-PCC (weight- and INR-based protocol) plus IV vitamin K, and re-check the INR after PCC. Plasma is the fallback when PCC is unavailable.
- **Dabigatran:** idarucizumab. If unavailable, PCC and consider dialysis.
- **Factor Xa inhibitor:** andexanet or 4F-PCC per institutional protocol. If surgery follows andexanet and heparin will be needed later, warn anesthesia and cardiac teams.
- **Unfractionated heparin:** protamine scaled to the heparin given recently. **LMWH:** partial reversal only.
- **Antiplatelet with surgery:** platelet transfusion and/or desmopressin per neurosurgery preference. Without surgery: no platelet transfusion (PATCH).

**Elective cranial surgery.** Neurosurgery counts as high bleeding risk. DOACs are held for longer when kidney function is reduced; bridging with heparin is usually unnecessary for DOACs and, for warfarin, BRIDGE showed bridging added bleeding without fewer clots in most atrial fibrillation patients. Mechanical mitral valves are a common exception.

**Pitfalls.**
- Forgetting vitamin K with PCC, leading to INR rebound and re-bleeding.
- Assuming a normal INR excludes a factor Xa inhibitor effect.
- Delays to wait for lab results when the history is clear.
- Thrombosis after reversal: restart prophylactic anticoagulation once the neurosurgeon judges hemostasis secure, and plan therapeutic resumption as a team.

The right answer is often a protocol agreed in advance by neurosurgery, hematology, pharmacy and the ICU.

keyPoints: Warfarin: 4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K (PCC alone rebounds)
Dabigatran: idarucizumab, a humanized Fab with far higher affinity than thrombin
Factor Xa inhibitors: andexanet alfa (decoy Xa; more thrombosis in ANNEXA-I) or 4F-PCC
Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin, only partially LMWH
PATCH: platelet transfusion harmed non-surgical ICH patients on antiplatelets
Speed matters because hematoma expansion happens in the first hours

test.explain: INR is insensitive to factor Xa inhibitors; drug-calibrated anti-Xa assays are needed.

test.q: Which drug can be partly removed by hemodialysis?
test.explain: Dabigatran has low protein binding and is dialyzable.

test.q: Name the positively charged protein that reverses heparin.
test.explain: Protamine binds negatively charged heparin.

test.q: PCC stands for prothrombin ___ concentrate.
test.explain: Prothrombin complex concentrate.

test.q: Which blood product supplies fibrinogen after thrombolytic-related bleeding?
test.explain: Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen.

kidTest.q: Blood thinners help stop:
kidTest.explain: They prevent dangerous clots.

kidTest.q: If someone on a blood thinner bleeds in the brain, doctors need:
kidTest.explain: A reversal agent undoes the blood thinner.

kidTest.q: Do all blood thinners use the same undo medicine?
kidTest.explain: Each type has its own reversal plan.

kidTest.q: Why must doctors act fast?
choices: Bleeding in the brain can grow quickly
kidTest.explain: Fast reversal limits bleeding.

kidTest.q: Doctors call the undo medicine a ___ agent.
kidTest.explain: A reversal agent stops the blood thinner from working.

advancedTest.q: After an andexanet infusion ends, anti-Xa activity can return because:
choices: Infused clotting factor X rapidly consumes the decoy, while apixaban itself is chemically destroyed and recreated by liver enzymes
Unbound inhibitor redistributes from tissues and andexanet binding is stoichiometric and temporary
The liver starts synthesizing new apixaban molecules
Andexanet converts into an anticoagulant metabolite
advancedTest.explain: The decoy works only while present.

advancedTest.q: A proposed contributor to andexanet's thrombotic signal is binding of:
choices: Antithrombin that blocks free thrombin and factor Xa
Fibrinogen required for the formation of fibrin strands
Vitamin K needed to produce functional clotting factors
advancedTest.explain: Removing TFPI lifts a natural brake on coagulation.

advancedTest.q: Why might hemostatic trials in ICH (FAST, TICH-2) reduce growth without clear functional benefit?
choices: Many patients were treated after most expansion had already occurred
Hematoma volume has no causal link to neurologic outcomes
Spontaneous intracerebral hematomas do not enlarge after presentation
Hemostatic drugs accelerate intracerebral hematoma growth
advancedTest.explain: Expansion is concentrated in the first hours; late treatment limits benefit.

advancedTest.q: For dabigatran, a normal standard thrombin time:
advancedTest.explain: Thrombin time is very sensitive to dabigatran.
